options: How an algorithm's cost grows as the input size grows, ignoring constant factors
The exact number of milliseconds an algorithm takes to run
How much memory a program uses on disk
The number of bugs an algorithm is likely to contain
questions.explain: Big-O describes growth rate as input size increases, not an absolute measured time, and it deliberately ignores constant factors.

questions.q: In the measured naive-vs-vectorized pairwise comparison, why were both versions still O(n²) despite the vectorized one being 15-22x faster?
options: The vectorized version actually used a different, lower-complexity algorithm
Both versions perform the same n² element comparisons; vectorization only reduced the constant factor per comparison, not the number of comparisons
The speedup numbers were measurement error and the two are really the same speed
NumPy secretly skips some of the pairwise comparisons
questions.explain: Both the naive loop and the broadcasted version compute all n² pairs; vectorization moves the per-element work into compiled code, shrinking the constant factor, but the growth rate as n increases is still O(n²) for both, as confirmed by the measured ~4x cost increase when n doubled.

questions.q: Why is an all-pairs correlation calculation over a universe of assets inherently O(n²)?
options: Because floating-point arithmetic is O(n²) by definition
Because pandas DataFrames are always O(n²) to construct
Because correlation requires sorting the data first
Because there are n² pairs to consider when comparing every asset against every other asset
questions.explain: Comparing every one of n items against every other item necessarily produces n² pairs, which is the source of the O(n²) cost regardless of how the comparison itself is coded.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the risk of only testing a pairwise algorithm on a small sample (e.g. 50 tickers)?
options: There is no risk; O(n²) algorithms scale the same at any size
The algorithm may look fast in testing but become the dominant cost once the real, much larger dataset (e.g. 5,000 tickers) is used, since cost grows quadratically
Small samples always produce incorrect results
Testing on small samples causes memory leaks
questions.explain: Because O(n²) cost grows with the square of n, a 100x larger input produces roughly 10,000x more pairwise work — a jump that's invisible when only testing on small data.

questions.q: Which operation is typically O(log n) rather than O(n)?
options: Binary search (e.g. `np.searchsorted`) on an already-sorted array
Summing all elements of an array
Computing the pairwise correlation matrix of n assets
A linear scan through an unsorted list looking for a value
questions.explain: Binary search on sorted data roughly halves the remaining search space with each comparison, giving O(log n) cost, far better scaling than an O(n) linear scan.
